title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
summary:
Use of global primary energy — naturally occurring energy sources that have not undergone any processing by humans — more than doubled between 1980 and 2025.
Although the share of primary energy generated by renewables is growing, oil, coal and gas still account for about 80% of energy production.
Source: Our World in DataThe IEA defines energy security as reliable, affordable access to all fuels and energy sources.
The IEA says that this could drop to $50 by 2035 and that geothermal energy could generate 8% of global electricity supplies by 2050.
Efforts to develop more efficient solar cells could also help countries to improve their energy security by increasing sustainable domestic electricity supplies.

title: Was Delhi pollution data during Diwali misleading?
summary:
BBC Verify has found significant discrepancies between two Indian government datasets showing Delhi's air pollution during Diwali, indicating official figures may not have captured the full extent of the problem.
But every hourly PM2.5 reading above 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre was excluded from the widely cited air quality index (AQI) published by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), even though these higher readings were present in the data from the Delhi Pollution Control Commission (DPCC).
Delhi is one of the most polluted cities in the world and often has dangerously poor air quality, so it is vital people living in India's capital can trust the official data.
But they can worsen air quality, especially in winter.
Government critics and opposition parties have accused the government of deliberately under-reporting the pollution data.

title: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change
summary:
Progress in each case, whether preventing dangerous climate change or stemming biodiversity loss, is too slow.
Now, the field offers strategies for protecting both climate and biodiversity from the many damaging effects of industrial agriculture.
Land clearance and land-use change contributes up to five billion tonnes of carbon annually — and is a major cause of biodiversity loss.
Advances in biotechnology that limit land use should be deployed to slow down the rise in global temperatures and biodiversity loss.
High-yielding crops produced using industrial agriculture have helped to feed the world but have also had a devastating effect on biodiversity.

title: Data centers need power – lower income, rural residents pay the price

With first author and postdoctoral researcher Cheng Feng, You also looked at data centers’ economic benefits, finding that each gigawatt of data center capacity can create 15,000 jobs across the economy, with an average 2,700 jobs directly associated with the data center (although not necessarily all on-site).
The major grids they studied encompass regions with the largest clusters of data centers, including the southern San Francisco Bay area; north Texas around Dallas-Fort Worth; the Midwest; and the mid-Atlantic region, including northern Virginia, where the biggest concentration of data centers has been built to date.

title: Early-life air pollution tied to worse lung function as a teen
summary:
University University of CopenhagenA new study finds an association between air pollution exposure early in life and lung function in children and adolescents.
Researchers combined detailed calculations of air quality at participants’ home addresses with repeated measurements of the children’s lung function throughout childhood and adolescence.
The researchers found that even relatively small differences in air pollution levels around the children’s homes were associated with small but measurable differences in lung function.
“Air pollution is one of the environmental factors where we know many of the sources and can take action.
Strengthening efforts to improve air quality at the European level would be advantageous,” says Pedersen.

title: Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood
summary:
Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil’s pristine wetlands and savannahs have ingested traces of plastic pollutants.
Researchers measured the concentration of microplastics in the blood of 47 animals: 26 lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) and 21 giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla).
The scientists found that, on average, the creatures carry similar levels of plastic as many humans — roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood.
The animals that lived closest to human infrastructure and waste-management facilities had the highest levels of microplastics in their blood.
To find out, Noonan, Ferraz and their colleagues collected and analysed blood samples from animals living across the Amazon rainforest, the Cerrado savannah and the huge and pristine Pantanal wetland between February 2021 and November 2022.
